IntroductionOne of the fundamental problems of system biology is to find the source of variation. Many researchers are interested in finding variation in various sources, for example, in-vitro cells. Moreover, in-vitro cells do not contain the complex cellular context and genome-wide context that occur in in vivo cells. The in-vitro experimental results are required to be reproduced in order to validate a finding. In this context, a reliable protein subcellular localization network serves as the molecular anchor for a reference genome. The aim of this study was to create a system to generate reliable spatial maps of protein subcellular localization networks.MethodsWe used the molecular landmarks provided by CellOGEN to characterize the expression of each cell type in all cell populations derived from a patient sample. These landmarks were generated by extracting the cytoskeletal genes from a microarray dataset. Each marker contains the three species of landmarks that represent the nucleus, cytoplasm, and the extracellular matrix. These landmarks are used as input for a powerful machine learning system to generate a protein subcellular localization network. Using this network, the most informative spatial region of each cell type can be identified.ResultsWe used this machine learning approach to generate a protein subcellular localization network. We used 197 markers representing different subcellular locations for each cell type. The feature selection algorithm gave us an average of 300 landmarks in each spatial region. These landmarks were useful for identifying the most informative spatial regions in each type of cell. Additionally, we showed that the level of expression for each marker was useful to identify the most informative spatial regions. Finally, we demonstrated that the network can be used to differentiate between benign and malignant cells from patient samples.ConclusionsThe network generated from CellOGEN provides a system to understand the spatial distribution of each protein from various cell types. Our method facilitates the identification of the source of protein subcellular localization networks and has potential to identify the sources of spatial maps of other cellular processes.

In the context of single-cell genomics, mapping genomic regions of interest (ROIs) to tissue-level phenotypes or sub-phenotypes is challenging. Characterizing these ROIs requires performing mapping of phenotype-defining genes (PFGs) on each chromosome, as the genes encoding these PFGs likely span multiple chromosomes. This paper focuses on a new algorithm, Phalgopter, which produces gene-based, annotated OMA sequences without the need for any prior reference to orthologous proteins. Phalgopter builds a kNN-style tree from the orthologous genes for a given organism. We estimate that Phalgopter can map ROIs 10-100x faster than with current C++ code and significantly more accurately than with traditional methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate how Phalgopter can be adapted to produce highly accurate predictions of relationships between genes, with a minimum of known annotations to refer to. These predictions can be used to identify which genes are functionally related to which genes by examining their expected change in expression following transfection with PFG plasmids. In addition, Phalgopter can be used to estimate the density of tissue-level features within an RNA-seq dataset at a spatial resolution as small as 50x50 cm2.

Unsupervised clustering of transcriptomes represents an important technique for the characterization of gene regulation in complex biological systems. Unsupervised clustering has received increasing attention for its potential to generate whole genome representations for non-uniform data samples from the same biological system, without the requirement for pre-existing training data. More recently, research has begun to highlight the potential of unsupervised clustering for disease representation. While previously, transcriptomic data were characterized using a single 'disease' dataset as a representative of the 'whole' population, recent emphasis is now being placed on the 'whole genome' representation. Here, we investigate the representational adequacy of transcriptomic datasets using unsupervised clustering. We evaluated the representational adequacy of seven publicly available unsupervised clustering algorithms using both a curated representation of two independent experimental disease datasets and a larger pooled human dataset representing a full panel of human diseases. We demonstrate that all the clustering methods investigated outperformed the standard clustering procedure, demonstrating the ubiquity of the problem of representation adequacy in unsupervised clustering. In addition, we observed that in the pooled human dataset we studied, clustering by its own performance strongly co-relates with the performance of datasets that include both 'disease' and 'non-disease' data samples. This result shows that although data representational adequacy is universal across clusters, some of these representational results are directly indicative of known biological phenomena, while others may represent non-signalling classes of sequences.

The Open Access version of this paper is available at https://openarchive.mdh.dk/handle/mdh/25678.

Human olfactory systems consist of hundreds of receptor genes linked to specific odorant binding sites, which in turn encode olfactory proteins which bind odorants. Research to date has largely focused on the roles of single genes in modulating olfactory receptor expression. Here, we use RNA-seq data to show that an expanded set of olfactory receptor expression genes contribute to modulation of olfactory receptor gene expression. Gene expression is often context-dependent and changes in cell population expression levels are highly variable. We hypothesize that these context-dependent changes are the result of competition between independently expressed olfactory receptor genes that possess weak binding affinity to odorants, and a broader set of genetic variants that can bind odorants with a higher affinity. The results show that, among these genetic variants, combinatorial loss-of-function variants were most strongly associated with increased olfactory receptor gene expression.

Gene expression profiling is a powerful tool that provides valuable insight into the genetic architecture underlying clinical phenotypes. Traditional approaches, however, primarily assess gene expression data, which is a limitation when assessing complex complex traits. The advent of mass cytometry (m/Mu_t) has opened up new avenues for the examination of gene expression and protein expression. We report the initial results of m/Mu_t data analysis of a robust gene expression dataset of 579,297 samples in 32 cell types. The analysis of the relationships between specific variants (single nucleotide variants, single-base pair variants, indels) and both gene expression and protein expression using m/Mu_t data demonstrates the accuracy of this method. The analysis of protein expression data based on 11,249 proteins demonstrates the powerful predictive power of m/Mu_t to provide insight into the pathophysiology of disease. Our results demonstrate that m/Mu_t enables the construction of complex trait score networks and genome-wide gene expression score networks. We discuss how these tools are useful in understanding disease and a potential future role for m/Mu_t in combining complex trait analysis and high-throughput molecular phenotyping of human cells.

There are numerous studies of cellular responses to drug exposures and chemical perturbation, and many epidemiological studies are informed by such experiments. However, estimating disease risk across multiple time points is a computationally costly endeavour. Because human transcriptional profiles change over time, the likelihood of such biological effects being uncovered at multiple time points arises naturally in a diverse range of scenarios. Here, we identify an integrated framework for estimating multiple biological effects of exposure across a single time point. We describe in silico methods to estimate multiple response biomarkers of exposure across multiple experimental time points using transcriptional profiles of the cell type (expression level, whole genome, and isoform level) and an external reference model. We also discuss the practical implications of our integrated methods.

One of the key challenges in unbiased biological data analysis is to extract structural information for a given biological function from single-cell transcriptomic datasets. This function is typically captured by so-called physical maps, which are intermediate measures of the impact of a given sequence variation on a cellular phenotype. This is particularly important for investigating novel proteins with functional role, since identifying the structures of novel proteins in cell's plasma membrane or nucleus is a major achievement for modern biology and a strong indication of a molecular functional change. In this study, we proposed the physical map utilizing least-squares 2D-correlation spatial filtering, which is a classical and widely used numerical software tool that has enabled us to analyze large-scale single-cell transcriptome datasets of various species, including humans. We constructed physical maps for neural precursor (OPN), part of RNA metabolism, which includes 14 physicochemical properties, including transmembrane topology, hydrophobicity, acyltransferase activity, and the 16-mer repeat sequences and demonstrated that the proposed map can discriminate phenotypic variants between two cell types as good as structural maps.

Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying phenotypic and ontogenetic transitions requires an assessment of a diverse array of phenotypic traits, and multiple transcriptomic measures are needed to account for the range of expression within a population. We developed a platform-agnostic approach for quantitative large-scale sequencing-based data generation, with high levels of gene expression variation measured across multiple tissue types or a tissue/organ. Our pipeline builds upon existing and well-established approaches, notably the BEAT project which pioneered the analysis of mRNA-level expression data in terms of its variation across tissue or organ types, and builds on them in a way that further improves efficiency and robustness. We developed a new model of transcriptome overlap based on recent advances in statistical analyses, and exploited the additional rich gene-level information to better capture isoform patterns, in particular, within mammalian tissues. Using transcriptomic data, we quantified the relationships between transcript isoforms and their potential to co-express in tissues, and illustrate the impact of isoform patterns on transdifferentiation and tissue-specific gene regulatory networks.

Currently, critical role of non-covalent interactions in the biology of membrane proteins is being discovered, which becomes the basis for cell signalling. The knowledge of non-covalent interactions is often hidden in the whole transcriptome. We used RNA-sequencing data from the SHOCK genes (coded in the PKS1-PKS2-PKS3 gene cluster) to create the "secretomescape" in the SHOCK-coding genes. We discovered a novel phenomenon in the interaction of SOS3-PKS1 with mRNAs of two different cellular components: human PAPES-2 and phosphatidic acid transport transporter (PATT)1. Further analysis of the interactions in the hidden genomic areas led us to further development of deep-learning-based network analysis to predict the 2D structures of SOS3-PKS1 in the SHOCK-coding genes based on the structure information from PKS1.

The fine tuning of gene expression during cell differentiation involves local changes in cell identity from an initially complex mixture of functionally homogeneous cell types to a small but highly specialized subset of cell states. Genome-wide sequencing (GWAS) has made it possible to characterize regions of DNA that regulate differentiation by identifying specific variants associated with each state. To identify these regulatory variants, researchers must perform complex statistical analyses using parametric and nonparametric statistics to identify regions of regulatory effect. This manual process consumes both time and resources and is prone to human error. Therefore, it would be beneficial to automatically generate GWAS regions to streamline data analysis, allowing for machine learning models to interpret the results. We propose an algorithm for identifying regulated regions based on SNP genotype data that outputs read-specific regions of the genome. We designed a method that takes the first 500,000 of read pairs and reconfigures them to facilitate characterization of differentially expressed regulatory regions. Our algorithm reduces the manual process of identifying regulatory regions to a well-defined set of criteria that are machine-readable. In our empirical evaluation, our method identified 50-60% of regulatory SNPs across a wide range of tissues and cell types, compared to manual approaches.
sample_p_texts: Typical mammalian overexpression systems test protein sequence variants with little control over expression levels and steady-state protein abundances, hindering interpretations of how protein sequence and expression converge to yield phenotypic outcomes. We explored the translation initiation sequence, commonly referred to as the Kozak sequence, as a means to modulate protein steady-state abundance and cellular function. We performed sort-seq on a randomized library of the 6 nucleotides preceding the start codon, amounting to 4,042 sequences. Calibrating the scores revealed a ~100-fold range of protein steady-state abundances possible through manipulation of the Kozak sequence. We identified human germline variants with predicted expression-reducing Kozak substitutions in disease-associated genes. Modulating the cell surface abundance of the host cell receptor ACE2 controlled the rate at which those cells became infected by SARS-like coronavirus spike pseudotyped particles. We demonstrated the potential of the approach by simultaneously testing Kozak libraries with a small panel of coding variants for ACE2 and STIM1. This approach lays the methodological groundwork for linking the causal relationships between protein sequence, abundance, and functional outcome.

MotivationDifferential expression analysis plays a vital role in omics research enabling precise identification of features that associate with different phenotypes. This process is critical for uncovering biological differences between conditions, such as disease versus healthy states. In proteomics, several statistical methods have been used, ranging from simple t-tests to more advanced methods like limma and ROTS. However, a flexible method for reproducibility-optimized statistics tailored for clinical omics data has been lacking.

ResultsIn this study, we developed LimROTS, a hybrid method integrating the linear model and empirical Bayes method from the limma framework with the Reproducibility-Optimized Statistics from ROTS, to create a novel moderated ranking statistic, for robust and flexible analysis of proteomics data. We validated its performance using twenty-one proteomics gold standard spike-in datasets with different protein mixtures, MS instruments, and techniques for benchmarking. This hybrid approach improves accuracy and reproducibility of complex proteomics data, making LimROTS a powerful tool for high-dimensional omics data analysis.

Availability and ImplementationLimROTS has been implemented as an R/Bioconductor package, available at https://bioconductor.org/packages/LimROTS/. Additionally, the code used in this study is available in GitHub repository https://github.com/AliYoussef96/LimROTSmanuscript

Allele-specific expression (ASE) is the imbalanced expression of two alleles of the same locus. It is quite pervasive among mammals and is associated with healthy and economically relevant traits. ASE is often used to support the identification of variants related to gene expression (cis-eQTLs). Thus, profiling ASE represents a significant step in elucidating the mechanism underlying gene expression regulation. In this study, we developed an ASE pipeline using public available RNA-seq data and open-source software. Using this pipeline, we were able to profile pervasive allelic imbalance across 42 tissues and 34 breeds from the Farm-GTEX-pig consortium at both SNP and gene levels without the need for parental genotype or whole genome sequence data. ASE was widely, but not evenly, spread across the genome. We also observed considerable variation in ASE profiles among various tissues, in which the ASE fraction ranged from 1.3% to 54.1%. ASE tends to be highly tissue-specific, and the overlap across tissues is limited. The functional analysis of tissue-specific ASE sites indicates that they are involved in the critical maintenance of these tissues. Our ASE pipeline can be readily applied to other RNA-seq data sets for livestock, thereby significantly expanding its potential utility. The wealth of available ASE resources provides a solid foundation for identifying regulatory elements within the genome that drive complex traits in livestock, making our pipeline and results valuable resources for researchers in this field.

Identifying differentially expressed transcripts poses a crucial yet challenging problem in transcriptomics. Substantial uncertainty is associated with the abundance estimates of certain transcripts which, if ignored, can lead to the exaggeration of false positives and, if included, may lead to reduced power. Given a set of RNA-Seq samples, TreeTerminus arranges transcripts in a hierarchical tree structure that encodes different layers of resolution for interpretation of the abundance of transcriptional groups, with uncertainty generally decreasing as one ascends the tree from the leaves. We introduce mehenDi, which utilizes the tree structure from TreeTerminus for differential testing. The nodes output by mehenDi, called the selected nodes are determined in a data-driven manner to maximize the signal that can be extracted from the data while controlling for the uncertainty associated with estimating the transcript abundances. The identified selected nodes can include transcripts and inner nodes, with no two nodes having an ancestor/descendant relationship. We evaluated our method on both simulated and experimental datasets, comparing its performance with other tree-based differential methods as well as with uncertainty-aware differential transcript/gene expression methods. Our method detects inner nodes that show a strong signal for differential expression, which would have been overlooked when analyzing the transcripts alone.

sample_q_texts: Examining spatial patterns of protein molecules, such as molecular communities or scaffolds, on a spatial network offers clues for complex biological mechanisms. To effectively analyze spatial protein clusters, it is essential to understand their evolution by identifying conserved subclusters, which collectively drive genetic evolution. However, selecting effective subclusters in large networks is challenging as most strategies rely on identifying networks of interest using evolutionarily conserved genes. In this study, we developed a model-free simulation framework called Hyper-Tac that simulates the evolutionary behavior of a large network using survival and mutation. We employed this framework to analyze evolutionary paths and divergence patterns of scaffold clusters with high protein levels. Our results show that subclusters involved in cellular processes have longer evolutionary trajectories, likely reflecting the evolutionary stability of subclusters rather than their specific genes. Specifically, we identified subclusters with evolutionary stability that are likely to be retained in a given ecosystem. This framework represents a powerful tool for analyzing evolutionary patterns of protein clusters and identifying scaffolds that contribute to the robustness of genetic evolution.

Proteins function via spatial and temporal interactions between proteins and other molecules within the cell. Determining which proteins interact with each other and how they are organized into functional networks is important to understanding their biological function. Currently, the statistical software tools available to measure how proteins associate are limited in their ability to represent the complexity of cellular organization. To address this, we propose the Virtual Genome Inference (VGI) algorithm. The VGI algorithm, developed with the Java framework Spark, builds a finite state automaton from gene and splice-level expression data. The automaton captures how genes interact with each other in subsets of the genome based on genetic variations. The resulting VGs show a high level of representation for protein networks. We evaluated the VGs against published transcriptional co-expression networks in various organisms, finding that our approach provided a functional inference solution to the problem of protein-protein interaction network reconstruction. The VGs can serve as a proof of concept for understanding how proteome networks emerge from gene interactions.

Network disease models provide valuable tools for characterizing the mechanisms of human disease, however, most approaches are primarily conceptual and do not explicitly model how information is propagated between cellular networks. To address this gap, we developed a computational model that defines circuit boundaries and routes within each cell in a network of physical proteins, known as electron transport (ET) proteins. This model allows us to model a specific protein transport pathway within each cell to study its effect on the network as a whole. In this study, we used this model to gain insights into the process of melanoma progression. Our results show that cancer progression requires the efficient binding and movement of ET proteins between cancerous cells as well as the regulation of tumor angiogenesis. Our work is the first to be able to explicitly capture and model the behaviors of individual proteins within each cell to facilitate insight into cellular disease mechanisms. This model will be useful for guiding treatments and drug development, and improving disease modeling.

Significance StatementElectron transport (ET) proteins are a small, diverse family of proteins that transport nutrients, oxygen, and waste around the body. One family of these proteins, called vesicular monoamine transporters, shuttle neurotransmitters across cell membranes and catalyze the transport of cellular oxygen. Cell-to-cell communication is mediated by many of these proteins, and we currently do not know how information is transmitted across cellular networks. In this study, we developed a computational model to study these processes in a real-world model of melanoma progression. The model allowed us to trace specific vesicles, or vesicles carrying neurotransmitters, within each cell of the tumor and show how the vesicles were regulated. This model will facilitate insights into the mechanisms of human disease and allow us to use it for drug development and understanding human biology.

Exploring complex processes in plants is a key challenge in modern biology. One approach that may provide insight into complex biological processes, particularly to understand how cells coordinate growth, development and morphogenesis is to study compartmentalized gene expression and signaling dynamics in response to external conditions. Transcription factors (TFs) that bind to promoters to promote transcription of genes to form cells or tissue types are a major class of TFs that regulate the compartmentalized transcriptional programs in cells. The current approach for studying TFs in different cell types involves expressing them transiently and quantitating the mRNA levels in different cell types. However, it has been difficult to have a clear understanding of how cell-type specific interactions determine how the TFs behave in different cell types. Recently, we performed stochastic simulations in a three-compartment mathematical model to analyze how transcription factor interactions and the strength of the TFs trans-acting properties of specific promoters affects transcription. We model the compartmentation of cells in different cell types in a stochastic model where we define intracellular compartments, individual promoter strengths and the population of TFs that are distributed among the compartments. We find that compartmentation strongly modulates the strength of TFs. We show that, in contrast to multicellular, fully differentiated cells, basal stem cells interact with their differentiated counterparts in more heterogeneous compartments in which differentiated cells interact with each other. Our findings show that the model we have developed provides a novel approach to understand the impact of compartmentation on TFs and TCF in living systems.

From single cell data, we are able to infer important biological processes, but they have no biological relevance. In this study, we applied causal inference (CII) to two cases, namely the loss of coordination and the redistribution of proteins to better reflect these biological dynamics. We applied three previously developed CII analysis, namely causal loop diagram (CLD), Bayesian structural network analysis (bSNAn), and differential analysis of gene expression (DAGs). We applied CLD to detect COVID-19 cell state changes during progression of the virus to the brain and find that the loss of coordination was present before the brain samples were collected. We assessed the causal links between protein pools and the cell state changes and observed that the redistribution of proteins to the nucleus is able to explain the loss of coordination for a single cell. The results are supported by DAGs and bSNAn. We conclude that by integrating causal inference into techniques used in multi-omics research, it is possible to identify critical processes occurring in a disease progression in a single cell.

Significance Statement
We have explored the question of how to better model the complex dynamics of cells, such as the immune system, to enable us to make better predictions. We examined two disease stages: The first stage is when COVID-19 infection disrupts the control of immune responses. The loss of coordination between the immune system and human biology can lead to several autoimmune diseases, including B cell lymphoma. The second stage is when T cells and B cells distribute proteins to the nucleus, such as interleukin 12. DAGs and bSNAn analysis of these two cases indicate that these two processes are associated. This indicates that integrating the causal inference approach into computational methods will provide better results.

Design for complex regulatory systems such as protein-protein interactions, gene regulatory networks and developmental pathways is a challenging yet critical task for the scientific community. To solve this challenge, this study proposes a framework for the automated identification of modules of regulatory logic, i.e. biologies, enabling the connection of protein-protein interactions, gene regulatory networks and developmental pathways. Using a custom-developed knowledge base of regulatory networks and gene regulatory networks, an experimental design strategy, termed co-selection, is proposed. It involves first identifying minimal modules in one parameter space, subsequently combining them and excluding redundancies, while simultaneously encouraging interactions within modules, achieving positive modular synergies in general. For the functional validation of the proposed approach, a representative modular integration scenario is considered, including a complete regulation of a model transcriptional system. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach is able to identify minimal modules combining regulatory patterns within a few clock cycles and combining/decomposing minimal modules with unexpected ones, to better reflect the current physiological state of a cell or organism. In addition, the minimal integration of these modules leads to synergistic outcomes that enhance cellular and developmental stability. These results are relevant for improving understanding of complex developmental pathways in plants, as well as in cellular models.

We identify key interacting pathways in gene expression networks and identify regulators of genes that are functionally and transcriptionally associated.

Crosstalk results in gene expression regulation of networks with co-expressed genes and likely functional properties. This reveals the essential information for a specific molecular process by modelling the non-invasive interaction between populations of cells. The goal is to construct a molecular machine which will be useful for informing biological questions in systems biology.

Crosstalks between genes with strong co-expression are often large. This co-expression interaction is largely ignored. In this work, we identify those genes that are transcriptionally and functionally associated and show how this information can inform the design of machine learning algorithms. It has been shown that the co-expression of genes in non-genetic networks with a common function can be informative. These insights are crucial to uncover new insights and inform future applications.

For a living cell to maintain a well-defined internal environment, multiple coupling pathways must work in unison. However, the composition of the microenvironment and the cellular environment itself can affect how signaling pathways are organized. This contribution aims to understand how the physical world and biological activity interact to regulate signaling through compartmentalization.

We carried out two experiments to test our hypotheses. The first experiment used an artificial environment comprising three compartments containing fluorescent molecules of different sizes that allowed us to monitor light absorption as a function of size. Our results revealed a 3-compartment model which simulates the functional physiology of cells.

In the second experiment, we imaged the entire interphase of a human cell by using a microfluidic system and single-molecule fluorescence microscopy to isolate its activity. Our results suggest that the same three-compartment model described in the first experiment co-exists with an additional compartment that controls the amplification of some reactions. Our data on the transcriptional regulator TERT was especially intriguing, as this molecule was inactive in one compartment of the microfluidic system but fully functional in the other. Together, these experiments reveal a more detailed model of how subcellular signals regulate signaling pathway organization and the cellular environment.

A previously described protein was initially found in a time-series protein interactome. For each protein, a unique knockout strain was generated in this series. A key observation was that there were significant functional differences between protein categories and temporal profiles of protein interaction activity. Here, a web-based resource was developed that allows users to visualize individual protein's interactions with high-dimensional structural parameters. This visualization serves as a tool to better explore temporal interactions, in particular, those of protein complexes.

The liver is an exceptional organ, consisting of approximately 2.5 million cells with several thousand genes, whose dynamic dynamics are characterized by massive turnover and complex patterns of transcription and translation. In particular, the presence of cells with different levels of activation (expression of specific proteins) within an organ can generate differential metabolic fluxes and signal input that modulates the flow of metabolic fluxes throughout the cell. A model that accounts for the possible dynamics of the gene expression is also described in the literature, however, we have seen in our studies that its robustness depends on parameters that are difficult to determine in vivo. To address this problem, we established a high-fidelity cellular in vitro system, where we can measure the expression levels of thousands of genes and genomes simultaneously in a spatially controlled way. Using this model, we have found that the model describes remarkably well the dynamics of the expression in a highly dissected part of an organ. We have also built a nonlinear time-series model that accounts for the possibility of being present of the genes at any moment of the cell. Furthermore, we have tested the model with real-time RNA sequencing experiments and show that it captures the measured levels of gene expression with a standard deviation of ~5%.
sample_p_texts: Computational models in systems biology are often underdetermined--that is, there is little data relative to the complexity and size of the model. The lack of data is primarily due to limits in our ability to observe specific biological systems and restricts the utility of computational models. However, there are a growing number of experimental databases in biology. While these databases provide more observations, they often do not have observations that match the system of interest exactly. Here, we investigate what information can be gleaned from these general databases in the context of modeling a specific system - cell signaling. Ultimately, our goal is to better determine models of specific systems, thereby increasing their utility. We use this framework to integrate measurements from the protein data bank (PDB) and UniProt (FASTA) and to quantify what information is gained from these measurements when modeling cell signaling. We choose to investigate the utility of these databases in the context of dynamic cell signaling models because experimental measurements of the variables of interest-- protein dynamics--are still quite limited. We find that we can successfully integrate measurements from these databases to improve parameter estimation of the cell signaling models. The impact of the database-derived measurements on model predictions depends on the complex relationship between model prediction and parameter values. Nonetheless, this study demonstrates that measurements from databases have the potential to be generalized to better inform parameters in models of cell signaling.

During manufacturing batches, Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells encounter critical levels of environmental stressors such as ammonia, lactate, and osmolality accumulation that can significantly reduce cell health and productivity. It is therefore crucial that stress adaptation and resistance be factored into cell line development (CLD). In this study, we employee population-based transcriptomic and differential gene expression analysis on stress-induced CHO cells to identify biomarkers displaying both heritable and stress-responsive properties. Using this workflow, 199 genes displayed transcriptional variability characteristic of a bistable system that formed four network communities of co-fluctuating genes. These communities were enriched in genes related to the regulation of apoptotic processes and gene expression/metabolic pathways. Seven genes were identified as promising biomarkers for engineering a stress-resistant phenotype. Genetic engineering methods may be employed in the future to bias clonal populations for higher stress tolerance to manufacturing stress, therefore increasing cell health and productivity in at-scale bioreactors.

Biochemical networks are models of biological functions and processes in biomedicine. Hierarchical decomposition simplifies complex biochemical networks by partitioning them into smaller blocks (modules), facilitating computationally intensive analyses and providing deeper insights into cellular processes and regulatory mechanisms. We introduce a novel algorithm for the hierarchical decomposition of large-scale biochemical systems. By using causality and information flow as organizing principles, our approach combines strongly connected components with r-causality to identify and structure manageable network blocks. Benchmarking against a comprehensive database of biochemical reaction networks demonstrates the computational efficiency and scalability of our algorithm. To ensure broad applicability, we integrate our algorithm into tools that support standardized Systems Biology Markup Language (SBML) formats, facilitating its use in biochemical modeling workflows.

Molecular interaction networks are a vital tool for studying biological systems. While many tools exist that visualize a protein or a pathway within a network, no tool provides the ability for a researcher to consider a proteins position in a network in the context of a specific biological process or pathway. We developed ProteinWeaver, a web-based tool designed to visualize and analyze non-human protein interaction networks by integrating known biological functions. ProteinWeaver provides users with an intuitive interface to situate a user-specified protein in a user-provided biological context (as a Gene Ontology term) in five model organisms. Protein-Weaver also reports the presence of physical and regulatory network motifs within the queried subnetwork and statistics about the proteins distance to the biological process or pathway within the network. These insights can help researchers generate testable hypotheses about the proteins potential role in the process or pathway under study. Two cell biology case studies demonstrate ProteinWeavers potential to generate hypotheses from the queried subnetworks. ProteinWeaver is available at https://proteinweaver.reedcompbio.org/.

The regulation of biological functions is achieved through the modulation of biochemical reaction network dynamics. The diversity of cell states and the transitions between them have been interpreted as bifurcations in these dynamics. However, due to the complexity of networks and limited knowledge of reaction kinetics, bifurcation behaviors in biological systems remain largely underexplored. To address this, we developed a mathematical method, Structural Bifurcation Analysis (SBA), which decomposes the system into substructures and determines important aspects of bifurcation behaviors--such as substructures responsible for bifurcation conditions, bifurcation-inducing parameters, and bifurcating variables--solely from network topology. We establish a direct relationship between SBA and classical bifurcation analysis, enabling the study of systems even in the presence of conserved quantities. Additionally, we provide a step-by-step bifurcation analysis for general use. We applied our method to the macrophage M1/M2 polarization system. Our analysis reveals that the network structure strongly constrains possible patterns of polarization. We also clarify the dependency of the M1/M2 balance on gene expression levels and predict the emergence of intermediate polarization patterns under gene deletions, including SOCS3, which are experimentally testable.

Our desktop application MBCO PathNet allows for quick and easy integration and visualization of networks of functionally related pathways predicted from numerous gene and protein lists using the Molecular Biology of the Cell Ontology (MBCO) and other ontologies. Within networks of hierarchical parent-child relationships or functional relationships, pathways are visualized as pie charts where each slice represents a dataset that predicted that pathway. Sizes of pies and slices can be selected to represent statistical significance or other quantitative measures. In addition, MBCO PathNet can generate bar diagrams, heatmaps and timelines.

sample_q_texts: Cultured human ESCs can develop from ESCs and embryonic stem-like (ESL) cells. However, ESCs are not cultivated for long without differentiation to any mature cell type, a critical step to meet the growing global demand for ESC-derived cell therapeutics. Here, we describe how a new "cellular platform," a cultivation-independent stem cell (CISC) platform, can be used to enrich and cultivate ESCs for cell differentiation to any mature cell type (human iPSC-derived cell types), while maintaining ESC identity.

ContextThere has been growing interest in using the middle ear-derived cells (MEDCs) as alternative source of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) for transplantation of marrow-derived MSCs (MDMSCs) into craniofacial or dental regions to replace lost or dysfunctional MSCs.However, MEDCs do not function in isolation. MEDCs come in clusters, which interact with host cells through a tight but also loose network and communicate through chemical, molecular, and communication pathways leading to complex and dynamic regulation of cell fate.Cells that are derived from a given cell type within a given organ will often differ from cells in other organs, and therefore have different immunogenicity and therefore tumorigenicity potential. Until now, there are no studies that address the effect of foreign mesenchymal cells, whether MSCs or not, within organs and cells that are implanted from different tissues from patients or have different tissue origins, on the tumors generated from cells or tissues within or attached to the host.

ObjectiveTo examine the immunogenicity and tumorigenicity of the foreign MEDCs and the transplanted tumor within the host.

MethodsCellular and molecular characterization of the MEDC-plant cell lines (derived from human medulloblastoma, glioblastoma, and glioblastoma cell lines in primary and organ cultures) were carried out using fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACs) and flow cytometry. Cell growth and differentiation were evaluated by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TND) assay, quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), and immunofluorescence microscopy. Tumorigenicity of MEDC-plant cell derived tumors, as measured by clonogenic response, proliferation rate, and histological parameters, were evaluated using clonogenic growth inhibition assay and cell cycle distribution. Stained tissues from patients were subjected to immunohistochemistry (IHC) of anti-VEGF and anti-CD31 antibodies. The immunogenicity of foreign tissues (in terms of tumor responses and clonogenic growth inhibition) and foreign cells (as determined using clonogenic growth inhibition and proliferation rate) were compared between in vivo (human medulloblastoma, glioblastoma, and glioblastoma cell lines, transplanted in the primary organ, the spinal cord, the cranial cavity, and the brain) as well as mouse (cloned glioblastoma cell lines in the primary organ, the spinal cord, the cranial cavity, and the brain) and rat (cloned glioblastoma cell lines in the brain) models. This study also evaluated the potential immunogenicity and tumorigenicity of humanized mouse T-cells.

Human stem cells have a clear potential to become differentiated cells with distinct, long-term fates, including cardiomyocytes for treating heart diseases. However, the lack of sufficient human stem cell populations with a defined heart phenotype has made it difficult to isolate and culture cardiomyocytes from patients undergoing heart biopsies. Here, we report a method to generate human-heart derived pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells. We are able to differentiate these cells into cardiomyocytes with functional features that are highly comparable to those of adult cardiomyocytes. The method we describe can serve as a reference for iPS cell-based biomedical research and can facilitate early approaches to assess the development of fully differentiated iPSCs, with the potential for applications in regenerative medicine and early therapeutics.

De novo, complete somatic cell replacement is a controversial and challenging method for therapeutic applications. The most crucial challenges for such an endeavor include cell-to-cell homing, cell reprogramming and genetic transformation. The latter is particularly complicated due to the complex regulatory circuitry underlying differentiated cell behavior. The research focuses on defining and improving some aspects of the genetic transformation process. We have developed a new method to generate transgenic stem cells from selected epithelial cell lines, by transient transfection of specific areas with transgenes encoding a viral vector that directs a transformation specific to the cellular source. Such a method enables transgene transfer to epithelial stem cells and therefore to be applied to develop in vivo reprogramming protocols for mesenchymal stem cells derived from adult mesenchymal progenitor cells.

Hierarchical clustering of 72 TCpl-derived stem cells shows a high degree of differentiation after clonal transformation. By removing the transgene-encoding transgenes, the cells lose their proliferative capacity, but they still express their primary transgene. Stem cell differentiation is prevented as a consequence of programmed cell death. In the absence of senescence, differentiation is associated with alterations of telomerase activity, stem cell migration toward the center of an epithelial mass and their division. Further characterization of the cells under the described conditions will shed light on how to better reprogram mesenchymal stem cells from adult populations.

Stromal fibroblast stem cells (SFSs) have the potential to differentiate into multiple lineages and contribute to various tissue regeneration processes, including tendon, heart, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue regeneration. The mitotic transition from SFS to mature myofibroblasts (MFs) in adult tendons is a complex process that is characterized by changes in the actin composition and overall phenotype. However, little is known about how SFSs within mature tendon structures maintain the coordinated mitotic transition from SFS to MF within the tendon cells. Here, we investigated whether SFS in mature tendon stem cells (mst-SFSs) contribute to the cell-autonomous maintenance of maturation in tendon cells. We identified three distinct cell states, MSCs (e.g., representing the fate-limited MSCs), STSs (e.g., representing the B cell lineage STSs) and SFS, respectively. Within mst-SFS, STSs were found to be activated only when mature MSCs and SFS in mst-MSCs, whereas only mature MSCs were required for SFS activation within mst-SFS. Our findings highlight the importance of maintaining critical mechanisms for the complete SFS-MF transition during development.

During myocardial regeneration, cardiomyocytes (CMs) undergo a spontaneous self-renewal process. However, what triggers CM self-renewal and autocrine regulation during the recovery process is unclear. Here, we studied CM self-renewal during recovery in the context of an ischemic heart injury by rearing CMs in the presence of inducible factors (IFNs) or angiogenesis inhibitors (ANIs). Experiments revealed that IFN-mediated CM self-renewal during ischemia in mice requires STAT5A, STAT4, and LIF but not JAK1/2. Additionally, CMs in ANIs displayed identical self-renewal capacity to those in IFN treatment. These results are compatible with the notion that both STAT5A and LIF act on both STAT4-dependent and LIF-independent pathways for CM self-renewal during injury. Lastly, we revealed that LIF expressed by endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) could regulate CM self-renewal and self-renewal capacity of both cardiomyocytes and fibroblasts, including MSCs. Together, our findings suggest that LIF may be a multifunctional cell signaling molecule that plays a central role in self-renewal of CMs and regulates the cellular adaptations to ischemia in heart injury.

HighlightsSelf-renewal of CMs during ischemia is regulated by STAT5A, STAT4, and LIF

We define somatic stem cell therapy as an experimental setting where stem cells are injected into target organs, such as muscles, after extensive mechanical loading of a given organ. We use a newly developed term somatic stem cell differentiation therapy to describe the procedure where stem cells are transplanted to the adult body to "inject the future". Even though many stem cell science concepts originated from cell biology, few animal models offer a systematical setup for this sort of treatment. To begin a somatic stem cell differentiation therapy, adult skeletal muscle is engineered to contain a transgene inducing reprogramming of the cells into neural stem cells. These neural progenitors are surgically harvested and transplanted into the muscle after exposure to mechanical loading. During transplantation, the targeted cell types differentiate during their maturation process, and express functional neural markers in muscle (e.g., NeuN, or dSND). Neural progenitors generate distinct populations of genetically reprogrammed cells that regenerate functional phenotypes in adult organisms. Thus, this study demonstrates how a somatic stem cell differentiation therapy can be integrated into a rigorous, well-controlled model.

In mammalian cell cultures, cell cycle kinetics and intracellular signaling pathways play pivotal roles in determining the dynamic evolution of the cells, impacting both normal cell growth and tumor progression. In this study, we used field-adapted STC177 (SC177) mouse stem/progenitor cells to investigate cell cycle kinetics and downstream signaling pathways. SC177 mouse stem cells were found to be able to proliferate in vitro with a diverse range of growth media with similar features to human primary human embryonic stem cells and primary human placental stem cells, which are known to be very sensitive to signals mediated by the Wnt-B-catenin pathway. The cells maintained one of the highest proliferative potentials ever reported for mouse embryonic stem cells and placenta stem cells, which are among the most powerful adult stem cell lines available in the world. SC177 mouse stem cells also expressed high levels of beta-catenin and high-affinity of Wnt-b-catenin signaling, and were able to self-renew stably over 35 passages. These features imply that SC177 mouse stem cells are a useful model for studying and investigating all aspects of the Wnt-b-catenin signaling pathway.

Stem cells hold great promise in tissue engineering, as they offer the capacity to generate functional organ tissues. In this study, we generated 12 adult stem cell lines (ACSLs) derived from adult hepatocytes (AH). All ASCLs have the capacity to differentiate into cardiomyocytes (CMs), endothelial cells (ECs), smooth muscle cells (SMCs), neural cells, hepatocytes, osteocytes, adipocytes, and immune cells. Treatment of ASCLs with mesenchymal (MS) or osteogenic (Os) signals upregulated the differentiation capacity of ASCLs, whereas inducers of vascular cell adhesion molecules (VCAM) resulted in the differentiation of ASCLs into neural cells. We confirmed these results using CRISPR-Cas9-mediated knockouts for YAP1, c-Myc, c-Jun, and SOX9 in ASCLs to reduce the mesenchymal signals, thereby improving the differentiation potential of ASCLs into functional tissues. MSC and OA signaling attenuated the mesenchymal differentiation when osteogenic signals were absent, indicating that these two signals are co-necessary for ASCLs to differentiate into certain tissues. Furthermore, we applied the concept of single tissue isolation (STI) to ASCLs derived from mouse livers as a new method to optimize the MSC/OA signaling, which allowed us to generate ASCLs from mice with a large number of skin appendages and a red blood cell-like pattern. We used the single ASCLs to generate an amniotic transplant for the successful implantation of a mouse fetus, the implantation of which was followed by a rapid development of the placenta, vessels, and kidney. ASCLs generated from livers of ten neonatal mice had rapid development and complex organogenesis, which provide insights into the multi-tissue differentiation capacity of ASCLs.

Significance StatementThe regenerative therapy has great potential in restoring function of failing tissues and organs. However, a successful application of regenerative therapy is still limited by the lack of understanding of underlying mechanisms. In this study, we have demonstrated that single ASCLs have the ability to regenerate complex organ systems. Our method of single ASCLs generation provides an opportunity to select what characteristics to control the differentiation of ASCLs into desired cell types. The application of single tissue stem cells to in-vitro and then in-vivo models can facilitate the development of personalized regenerative medicine for the regeneration of specific organs.

Adult human stem cells have the ability to undergo spontaneous differentiation into non-embryonic adult tissues. To date, this phenomenon is considered a rather rare phenomenon and its precise mechanisms are not well understood. Here we provide a genome-wide characterization of spontaneous differentiation in human pluripotent stem cell lines based on genetic and epigenetic transitions, as well as gene expression changes associated with differentiation in a human organoid model. Using single-cell analysis, we identified three distinct progenitor cell populations within hPSC lines, demonstrating gene expression changes associated with developmental stages. The differentiation status of each cell population was assessed by gene expression, transcriptional activity and epigenetics signatures based on genome-scale gene expression profiling using a large set of cell-lines. Our results reveal two distinct stemness states in hPSC lines, the mesendoderm state (hPSC_MESD) and the embryoid body state (hPSC_EBODY), and reveal the transition from one state to another as occurring during clonal expansion. The transition status was further characterized in an organoid model derived from an adult hPSC line. Analysis of the transcriptomes and epigenomes of the tissue-specific organoid revealed cell identity-specific genes associated with tissue-specific adult stem cell states. Our analysis reveals the complex nature of the transcriptional regulation during stemness conversion in adult stem cells and provides an improved understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying the transition from one stemness state to another.
